1: Jakarta's sky at the end of 2048 stretched clear, a rare sight. As if the universe itself exhaled in relief after a series of storms battered President Nisa Farha's ship of leadership. Four years had slowly passed since justice's gavel struck at the Parliament building, passing the Family Readiness Bill — a monumental legislative product born from Nisa's burning concern over the fragility of Indonesian family foundations. Four years that felt like a decade full of turmoil. During that time, she and Reza Satria, her husband, not only led a plural nation, but also fought hard defending personal integrity, policy vision, even the wholeness of their own marriage from repeated attacks.

Now, on the Palace pavilion's shady balcony, Nisa Farha gazed at the dusk horizon. That place had become a silent witness to so much laughter, tears, strategic discussion until late at night, and moments of restorative intimacy. The fine lines around her eyes might be a bit more visible now; several silver gray strands now adorned her jet-black hair. That was the map of a leader's journey who never wavered facing storms, the trace of time, and the unavoidable burden of responsibility. However, her gaze radiated a different calm and depth, a wisdom born from being forged by trials. Her spirit's flame still burned, but now more stable. Its light more directed, no longer easily provoked by cheap provocation or swayed by momentary political ripples.

Reza approached her from inside, bringing two cups of warm unsweetened jasmine tea — their afternoon ritual never skipped, a small anchor amid the boundless sea of busyness. He wrapped his arm tightly around Nisa's shoulder, his chin resting gently on the top of his wife's head. The silver gray at his temples had also increased, but his smile now more often bloomed sincerely, returning faster after facing small ripples of media attack or political jabs that still occasionally appeared. The “let them be” principle Nisa had once tried teaching him had now become ingrained in him, giving him strength to choose his battles wisely.

“Twenty-three years of our marriage next week, Sa,” Reza whispered softly, breaking that peaceful silence. “And almost five full years you've led this country. It feels… like just yesterday we stood here, at the start of the first term, full of big dreams and… maybe a little too naive about how cruel this political world is.”

From the next room, the faint remains of laughter from a video call that had just ended could be heard — Alex, their only son now studying Environmental Engineering with a focus on renewable energy research in Germany, had just talked at length about his lab research, his Indonesian accent starting to mix with German-English. That interest had grown since childhood, from visits he often joined with Reza to various clean energy startups their family funded — a small seed slowly taking root as his own life path. Nisa smiled hearing it earlier from a distance, a warm reminder that behind the Palace's hustle, there was a small family life they still tended in their own way.

Nisa smiled slightly, lifting her head a little to look at her husband's face. “Yes,” she answered softly. “We've been through so much together, Za. Far more emotional turmoil than I ever imagined.” She let out a long breath, a breath of relief, no longer the exhaustion or despair that once pressed so heavily. “The endless political storm, the slander tsunami that nearly drowned us, the lightning of controversy from every new policy, even the poisonous whispers from a venomous snake in this very Palace corridor.” She referred inwardly to Rahmat Iskandar, the figure whose betrayal had almost ruined their communication and trust, now just a footnote in their Palace's internal history.

Their journey was indeed like a modern epic. The Family Readiness Bill, though its implementation still needed tight guarding, had begun showing its fruit. Central Statistics Agency data showed an 18% decline in early divorce rates among couples married after the law took effect. The national average marriage age rose 1.5 years, and women's gross enrollment rate in higher education increased 12%, giving young women more room to pursue education and independence before entering marriage's gate. The National Commission on Violence Against Women's report recorded a 22% decline in new domestic violence cases among young couples. Even public opinion surveys showed 55% of society now agreed on the importance of mental, emotional, and financial readiness before marriage — a significant social norm shift. “This isn't just numbers, Mas,” Nisa had once said to Reza while looking at that report, “This is a story of hope realized, a better future for millions of families.”

Then there was the National Movement “Bold Spark, Guard the Values,” an initiative born from Nisa's concern over the 'confidence deficit' and 'inferiority mentality' locking up the nation's creative potential. Its journey was no less steep. Andi Saputra's plagiarism scandal and the controversy over Bima the street musician's lyrics once shook that movement's foundation, triggering political attack from Pak Hardiman and whispers of doubt from within the coalition. However, with strategy adaptation, tightening of the “Guard the Values” pillar, and stories of resilience from creators like Maya, the illustrator whose work broke into international competition; Ibu Ningrum, the layered cake entrepreneur who rose from cyberbullying trauma; and even Bima himself who began finding his more mature authentic voice, that movement slowly found its rhythm. The safer, more interactive Bold Stage Digital 2.0 platform had been launched, proof of a bitter but necessary evolution.

And most monumental, of course, was legal and judicial reform. Triggered by Siti Rahayu's tragic case in Sulawesi and Dito Nugraha's in Kalimantan — two human beings who became victims of a broken system — Nisa took the biggest political gamble by nominating Ratna Dewi, former KPK Director of Investigation known for steel integrity, as Attorney General. That nomination triggered a political earthquake, intimidation, and a brutal war of nerves. However, with Nisa's full support and Ratna Dewi's own resilience at the House Commission III fit-and-proper test, that nomination was finally approved, and the Saber Peradilan Task Force soon moved — their first sting operation against a High Court Judge with initials AS had just shaken the judicial world weeks ago. Ratna Dewi hadn't even served a full month yet, and the road ahead was still long: case backlogs at the Supreme Court still mounted, resistance from within the institution hadn't fully subsided. But the direction was clear, and for Nisa, this was just the beginning of a gamble whose results would be reaped years ahead.
“A bold beginning,” Reza said, gently stroking Nisa's hair. “Fundamental change like this indeed needs time, needs revolutionary patience.”
Nisa nodded. “The homework is still very long, Za. Changing an already-rooted mindset, fighting cultural resistance, ensuring budget isn't misused. Sometimes I feel the progress is so slow.”
“But there is progress, right?” Reza affirmed. “And you never stop trying, never give up on your initial vision, even though storms keep coming in turn.”

They fell silent, enjoying togetherness in the dusk's quiet. The frequency of new harmony in their relationship felt so real. More honest communication about each other's fragility. New boundaries protecting their safe space. Laughter that returned to be heard often. Physical intimacy that was calmer, deeper, but no less strong. They'd learned again that openness and honesty must keep being tested and renewed; that being true partners means being each other's anchor in storms, reminding each other, strengthening each other, and forgiving each other.

However, amid the peace they'd begun to feel, a seed of new unease began growing in Nisa's heart. The success of the Family Readiness Bill now becoming widely known invited world attention: one by one delegations from other countries came to the Palace to study Indonesia's family reform model, and several international forums began inviting Nisa to share her experience. That attention opened her eyes to a scale of problems far wider than she'd ever imagined. Letters and emails began arriving at the Palace, not only from Indonesian citizens, but also from individuals in various parts of the world. Sorrowful stories about forced marriage in South Asia, about women shackled by repressive tradition in the Middle East, about young couples in Europe who'd lost direction and meaning in their relationship despite living in material freedom, about the epidemic of loneliness amid the crowds of big cities in America.

One night, after returning from an international forum where she shared about the importance of mental and emotional readiness in building strong families, Nisa couldn't sleep. She sat at the edge of the pavilion bed, looking at Reza sleeping soundly beside her. Her husband's face looked peaceful, far from the tension that once often colored his sleep. Nisa was grateful for that peace, a peace they'd fought hard together for. But her own heart was now filled with new ripples.

She rose slowly toward the small bookshelf in the room's corner, her finger tracing the spines of books she rarely touched anymore since being busy with state affairs. She stopped at one worn dark-blue-covered volume, far more tattered than the others — the first printed manuscript of a novel she'd written herself over a decade ago, long before she knew Reza, long before the word “President” had ever crossed her mind about the future. Algorithm City.

She smiled slightly, bitter yet amused, opening the pages that had begun yellowing. Lyra and Orion — two names born from the unease of a single woman in her mid-twenties, who at the time could only pour her anger at a world she thought valued efficiency more than feeling, into the form of science fiction about love seized by the system. AKGS that matched partners through cold calculation. DKE that punished anyone daring to feel too deeply. A fictional world that, she realized now, wasn't entirely fictional — just a more extreme version of what millions of real Aishas and Kenjis truly experienced in the real world, whose letters had recently begun filling the Palace's inbox.

Freedom to feel, to choose, to love each other unconditionally. The last line she'd written for Lyra and Orion, years before she knew that sentence would become more than just the closing of a teen novel almost no one read.

Nisa closed that book slowly, hugging it briefly to her chest. It felt like meeting again with a younger version of herself, who was angry at the world in the only way she knew then: writing. She never imagined that small anger would grow this big.

“Mas,” she whispered the next morning as they enjoyed breakfast at the small table in the pavilion's corner — a gadget-free, work-free zone now their sacred ritual. “Last night I read a UN Women report about global child marriage and gender-based violence rates. Reza set down his coffee cup, looking at Nisa attentively. “Yes, I also saw some of the infographics. The world is indeed still far from ideal, Sa.”

“Not just far from ideal, Mas,” Nisa shook her head slowly. “It feels like… we've only just cleaned one small corner of a very big, messy house. That unease kept haunting her. She began intensely exchanging thoughts with Reza, often until late at night. They discussed again their personal experience, not only as husband and wife, but also as two individuals who'd gone through various phases of spiritual and emotional growth. Nisa remembered her past writings, before political hustle consumed all her energy, about the importance of self-love, about how finding true happiness can't be hung on another person. “You have to accept and love yourself first before seeking a partner and building your love life,” a quote she'd once read and that had left such a mark, now echoed again.

Reza, in his calm and supportive way, listened to all of Nisa's unease. He also reflected on their journey. He remembered how openness and honesty in communication, including about biological needs often considered taboo, became one of the strongest adhesives in their marriage. He remembered how the two of them always tried to “not have many secrets,” and how the commitment to keep “learning to understand each other” became the key to getting through various differences and changes.

“I read about your vision to 'liberate body, soul, and knowledge',” Kenji wrote in fluent English. “I wonder, can my and my wife's soul still be 'liberated' at our no-longer-young age? Is there a way to reignite a long-extinguished flame, or are we indeed destined to live the rest of our life in this false warmth?”

Nisa and Reza discussed Kenji's case at length. This was a different challenge. Not about physical coercion or explicit cultural pressure, but about emptiness of meaning and the death of connection in a long-term relationship. They realized their “Global Love Therapy” also had to be able to answer the needs of couples like Kenji and his wife. The YCMG team then designed a special online module titled “Rediscovering Love's Frequency: A Guide for Long-Term Couples,” containing practical tips on empathic communication, new ways to build emotional and physical intimacy, and the importance of continuing to grow and explore together with a partner even at no-longer-young age. Kenji became one of the first participants in that module's pilot program.

Then, there was also testimony from a teenage boy named David, from a small town in the American Midwest. David, only 16 years old, wrote about his confusion facing pressure from his peers to soon have a girlfriend and be sexually active, though he himself felt not ready and more interested in his hobbies in music and science. He felt something was wrong with him for not being “like typical teenage boys.” He was afraid of being considered weird or not “manly.”

“I read an article about Ibu Nisa who once also felt comfortable being single and focused on self-development,” David wrote. “Is it wrong if I don't want to date yet? Do I have to force myself just to be accepted by my environment? I want to know how to 'liberate my soul' from this peer pressure.” David's case touched Nisa personally. She remembered the principles in “Finished With Myself First” so relevant: “Your life is more than just marriages, families… the main topic and milestone is and is ABOUT yourself.” The YCMG team, through their discussion platform, connected David with a peer mentor from their global network who also had similar experience, and gave access to material about the importance of self-love, recognizing personal boundaries, and daring to be different. The main message was: there's nothing wrong with being yourself, and readiness to enter a romantic relationship is a personal journey that can't be forced by others' standards.

These stories, and hundreds of others continuing to flow in every day, became the main fuel for Nisa and Reza. They saw directly how the “Liberated Love” vision resonated with human needs in various parts of the world. The “Voice of Liberated Love” platform not only became a place to vent, but also began transforming into a global community supporting each other. Users began exchanging comments, giving encouragement, sharing tips, and even forming small discussion groups based on shared issue or geographic region.

Nisa and Reza also began their first “Liberated Love Dialogues.” The initial destinations they chose were several Southeast Asian countries: the Philippines, Thailand, and Cambodia. In Manila, they met with a women's activist group fighting against the high rate of domestic violence and child marriage. Nisa shared her experience fighting for the Family Readiness Bill in Indonesia, giving inspiration and advocacy strategy. Reza spoke to husbands and male community figures about the importance of changing patriarchal mindset and becoming agents of change in family and community. In a remote village in northern Thailand, they sat cross-legged listening to stories of minority tribe women often victims of human trafficking disguised as marriage. There, the “Liberated Body” pillar felt so relevant and urgent. YCMG, through their partner in Thailand, committed to supporting economic empowerment and legal education programs for women in that village.

In Phnom Penh, Cambodia, they held an interactive workshop with a group of students and young professionals about “Building Healthy Relationships in the Digital Era.” Discussion ranged around social media pressure, ghosting, the importance of assertive communication, to how to maintain emotional intimacy amid career busyness. Nisa and Reza didn't appear as lecturers, but as facilitators, sharing their personal experience, answering questions honestly, and encouraging participants to find their own answers.

Every trip, every dialogue, further strengthened their conviction. The problem was real, the suffering universal, but hope and potential for change were equally great. They saw how the principles they'd formulated — the importance of open communication like in “The Flame That Never Dies,” appreciation of the body and partner's uniqueness like in “Gratitude for Love,” union of physical and spiritual aspects in intimacy like in “Union of Body and Soul,” and the power of self-love and self-resolution before marriage like in “Finished With Myself First” — turned out acceptable and applicable in various cultural contexts, though needing high adaptation and sensitivity.

Of course, this journey wasn't always smooth. In several countries, dialogue's door remained tightly shut. There were suspicious governments, religious groups strongly rejecting, local media twisting their message. Nisa and Reza learned to be patient, to not force their will, and to keep seeking small gaps where seeds of change could be planted.

Once, in a Q&A session after a seminar at a university in Kuala Lumpur, a hijab-wearing student with a critical gaze asked, “Ibu Nisa, Pak Reza, your vision of 'Liberated Love' sounds very idealistic, maybe even too Westernized for us living in a strong Islamic cultural context. How do you balance the individual freedom you fight for with religious values and tradition also important to us?”

Nisa smiled. This was the question she'd been waiting for, a very fundamental question. “Thank you for your very important question,” Nisa answered. “Let me assert, the 'Liberated Love' we mean isn't boundless freedom violating noble religious or cultural values. On the contrary, we believe the true essence of any religion's teaching, including Islam, is love, compassion (rahmah), justice, and appreciation of every human's dignity.”

She continued, “Coercion in marriage, domestic violence, or relationships hurting each other and not bringing to soul calm (sakinah), actually contradicts those fundamental values. 'Liberated Body' means guarding the body's trust given by God, not hurting and not being hurt. 'Liberated Soul' means having inner calm, free from fear and pressure, so one can worship and live life more devotedly. And 'Liberated Knowledge' means seeking beneficial knowledge, including knowledge about how to build a sakinah, mawaddah, warahmah family, according to religious guidance yet also relevant to the era's challenges.”

Reza added, “We believe that a lawful marriage bond, founded on conscious choice, sincere love, mental and spiritual readiness, and commitment to grow together, is a very noble act of worship. And in that bond, physical and spiritual intimacy can become a path to draw closer to the Creator, achieving the true 'heavenly gift and pleasure.' This isn't about imitating Western culture, but about digging up again the universal wisdom present in every noble tradition, including Islamic tradition, and applying it in the context of modern life.”

Nisa's and Reza's answer, balancing universal freedom principle and respect for local values, received wide appreciation. They showed that “Liberated Love” wasn't a threat, but an offer for reflection and growth together.

The first stories of liberation, from Aisha in Pakistan, Kenji in Japan, David in America, to dialogue participants in Southeast Asia, began being woven by the YCMG team into a global narrative. Not as a success claim, but as proof that hope existed, that change was possible, and that every voice, however small, was worth hearing.

That global resonance had just begun. Nisa and Reza knew, this would be a lifelong journey. However, seeing sparks of hope beginning to light in various parts of the world, they felt their energy seemed endless. They were the “World's Love Doctor Couple,” and the world, with all its wounds, was waiting to be healed, one heart, one relationship, at a time.
5: The initial resonance from “Voice of Liberated Love” and “Liberated Love Dialogues” indeed brought a wave of hope and validation for Nisa and Reza. Individual stories from various parts of the world longing for liberation and enlightenment in matters of the heart affirmed their vision's universality. However, as the Cinta Merdeka Global Foundation's (YCMG) reach expanded, they also began confronting head-on the towering walls of complexity. That challenge was no longer just sporadic skepticism or criticism, but resistance rooted in cultural, legal, and social systems in various countries.

One of the first biggest challenges they faced was the diversity of cultural interpretation toward the concept of “love,” “marriage,” and “individual freedom.” What was considered “liberation” in one cultural context, could be seen as “a threat to social order” or “destructive Westernization” in another cultural context.

For example, when the YCMG team tried developing an educational module about the importance of consent at every level of romantic and sexual interaction, they found that the concept of individual consent, especially for women, often clashed with arranged marriage practice still strong in many communities in South Asia and parts of Africa. There, marriage was often not just a matter of two individuals, but an alliance between extended families, where the bride-to-be's voice, especially women's, was often ignored or considered irrelevant compared to the family or clan's collective interest.

“How can we talk about consent for sexual relations, if consent to marry itself is often absent?” complained a women's activist from India in an online consultation session with Nisa and the YCMG team. “Here, refusing an arranged marriage set by parents can mean social ostracism, even threat of violence in the name of 'family honor'.”

Nisa reflected deeply on this. She remembered how in Indonesia too, before the Family Readiness Bill was rolled out, similar practice still occurred often, though maybe not as extreme as in some other places. She realized a “one size fits all” approach wouldn't work. YCMG's educational material had to be adaptable, “translated” into local cultural language, and delivered through figures or institutions respected in that community.

“We can't come as 'saviors' who feel we know better,” Nisa said in a YCMG strategy meeting. “We have to become dialogue partners. Seeking common ground between universal human rights values and local wisdom that might also have concepts of justice and compassion, though articulated differently. Maybe we need to involve more anthropologists, sociologists, and progressive local traditional or religious figures in designing our material and approach.”

Reza added, “And we have to be very careful not to seem judgmental or belittling tradition. Our focus is on the negative impact of certain practices on individual wellbeing, especially women and children, not on the tradition itself entirely. We offer perspective, not coercion.”

Another challenge emerged when the “Liberated Soul” pillar emphasizing the importance of self-love and emotional independence, as inspired by “Finished With Myself First,” was introduced in very communal and collectivist societies. In several East Asian or Latin American cultures, for example, excessive emphasis on “self” could be considered selfishness or neglect of family responsibility.

“The concept of 'resolve yourself first' is sometimes hard to accept here,” explained a psychologist from South Korea who became a YCMG partner. “Our society very much emphasizes group harmony and filial duty to parents. The idea of prioritizing personal happiness over family expectation often creates extraordinary inner conflict, especially for the younger generation.”

To address this, the YCMG team had to reformulate the “self-love” message into something more aligned with communal values. They emphasized that an individual with a healthy, stable, emotionally independent soul would actually be able to contribute better to their family and community. “Self-love doesn't mean becoming narcissistic or abandoning responsibility,” Nisa explained in a YCMG podcast aimed at global audience. “But about building a strong internal foundation so we can interact with others from a position of strength, not from a position of need or fear. A liberated soul is a soul able to give and receive love more sincerely, without having to lose itself.”

Next, the “Liberated Body” pillar covering comprehensive sexuality education and reproductive rights faced the thickest wall of resistance, especially from conservative religious groups in various parts of the world. YCMG's effort to promote understanding of healthy, safe, and consensual sexuality, and access to information about contraception or reproductive health services, was often labeled “amoral propaganda,” “a secular agenda destroying the young generation,” or even “a conspiracy to reduce the believing population.”

In one Middle Eastern country, YCMG's online material on body anatomy and reproductive function, neutral and scientific, was blocked by the government citing “contrary to public decency values.” In several US states dominated by conservative evangelical groups, YCMG's program trying to cooperate with schools to give inclusive sexuality education was flatly rejected by school boards and parents.

“This is a real ideology battlefield,” Reza said in a discussion with Nisa, his expression looking concerned. “We're not just fighting ignorance, but also fighting narrow interpretation of religious teaching often used to control women's bodies and perpetuate inequality.” Nisa let out a long sigh. She remembered how in Indonesia too, the fight to include reproductive health education in school curriculum was always colored by fierce debate. “We mustn't retreat, Mas,” Nisa answered firmly. “But we also can't attack frontally. We have to find allies from within the religious community itself. Religious figures with progressive and humanist views, who understand that guarding the body and soul health of believers is part of noble religious teaching.”

YCMG then began initiating “Interfaith Dialogue for Liberated Love,” inviting theologians, ulama, pastors, monks, and scholars from various religious traditions to discuss how universal values like compassion, justice, consent, and appreciation of human dignity could be found and strengthened in each religion's teaching, and how those values could become a basis to promote healthy and liberating relationships. The process was slow and full of challenge, but several initial dialogues began showing a glimmer of hope for common ground.

Besides cultural and religious challenges, YCMG also had to confront corrupt legal and political systems not siding with victims in many countries. The “Liberated Body” vision covering freedom from domestic violence or “Liberated Soul” covering the right to divorce from a hurtful marriage, often hit unresponsive law enforcement officers, gender-biased judges, or absence of adequate protection law.

In a Sub-Saharan African country, the YCMG team accompanied the case of a young woman experiencing severe domestic violence from her husband. Though physical violence evidence was very clear, that woman's report to local police was ignored with the reason “that's a household matter, no need to make a big deal.” Even, several traditional figures in her village actually blamed the woman for being considered “disobedient to her husband.” “This is frustrating,” complained Anton Prasetya in his report to Nisa. “We can give counseling and psychological support to victims, we can give them knowledge about their rights. But if the legal system in their own country doesn't protect them, all our effort will be in vain. Victims will return to the same cycle of violence.”

This experience made Nisa and Reza realize their third pillar, Advocacy and Systemic Change, had to run alongside the other two pillars. YCMG couldn't just focus on individual empowerment, but also had to dare push structural change. They began allocating more resources to support local legal NGOs fighting for law reform related to domestic violence, child marriage, and divorce. They also began using their global platform to raise legal injustice cases to world attention, giving international pressure to negligent governments. This was a risky step, which could make YCMG considered a political organization and invite hostility from several countries. However, Nisa felt this was a risk that had to be taken. “There's no true liberation of love without legal justice,” she asserted.

Complexity also came from YCMG's own internal dynamics. Their increasingly large and culturally diverse team also had its own challenges in communication, coordination, and shared understanding of the vision. There were differences in work style, expectation, and sometimes even interpretation of the “Liberated Love” principles themselves. Nisa and Reza had to learn to become global leaders able to manage this diversity, facilitate healthy internal dialogue, and ensure everyone stayed on one frequency of struggle.

Reza, with his business background, helped a lot in building a more professional and efficient foundation management and operational system. He emphasized the importance of accountability, fund usage transparency, and clear impact measurement for every program. “Idealism alone isn't enough, Sa,” he told Nisa. “A movement this big also has to be managed with high-level professionalism so it can be sustainable and trusted by donors and beneficiaries alike.”

One difficult decision they had to make was when one very enthusiastic “Liberated Love” facilitator in a Southeast Asian country, because of his own interpretation perhaps too literal of the “liberated body” concept, began promoting a very permissive view about premarital sex to underage teenagers without considering the very strict local cultural and legal context. This triggered great anger from parents and community figures, and nearly got YCMG's entire program in that country forcibly closed by the government. Nisa and Reza had to immediately step in, make clarification, apologize for the misunderstanding that occurred, and reassert that “Liberated Love” always ran alongside the “Guard the Values” principle — responsibility, ethics, and respect for applicable legal and social norms, though they also kept fighting to reform norms considered unjust. That facilitator finally had to be deactivated, a painful but necessary decision to maintain the movement's integrity and sustainability overall. This became a bitter lesson for YCMG about the importance of very careful training and continuous oversight for their field facilitators.

Amid all that challenge, Nisa often remembered her struggle in Indonesia. She remembered how the Family Readiness Bill also faced strong cultural resistance. She remembered how the “Bold Spark, Guard the Values” Movement nearly collapsed from scandal and political attack. Those experiences, though painful, had forged her into a more resilient, wiser, more patient leader. “We mustn't be discouraged, Mas,” Nisa told Reza one night, after a full day of marathon virtual meetings with YCMG teams from various time zones, discussing various obstacles and challenges emerging. “Remember when we almost gave up on the Family Bill before? Or when 'Bold Spark' was hit by storm? We succeeded getting through it because we never stopped learning, adapting, and most importantly, because we never lost conviction in our initial vision.”

Reza smiled, embracing his wife's shoulder. “You're right, Sa. Every challenge is a chance to make our movement stronger, more relevant, and more grounded. This global complexity actually forces us to think more creatively, more inclusively, and more humbly.”

They began developing a more layered and contextual approach. For very conservative societies, YCMG might focus first on more easily accepted issues, like the importance of family communication or domestic violence's danger from a child health and wellbeing perspective, before gradually introducing more “radical” concepts like individual right to choose a partner or sexuality education.

They also increasingly realized the importance of building “cultural bridges.” YCMG began actively seeking and collaborating with local artists, writers, filmmakers, and musicians in various countries to translate “Liberated Love” messages into forms of cultural expression more easily accepted and understood by local society — for example through short films, songs, traditional theater performance, or even comics and graphic novels.

One quite successful collaboration was with a group of women screenwriters in Egypt. Together, they developed a TV drama series idea raising stories of modern women in Cairo struggling to balance family tradition demands, religious values, and their personal aspirations for love and career. That series, though drawing some criticism from conservative groups, turned out to receive very positive reception from young female viewers throughout the Arab world, triggering important discussions about women's role in society and their right to determine their own life path.

Facing global complexity was indeed exhausting. Every day was a new battle, every culture a new labyrinth that had to be explored carefully. However, Nisa and Reza, together with the increasingly solid YCMG team, kept moving forward. They learned that being the “World's Love Doctor Couple” wasn't about having all the answers or forcing one single solution. Rather about becoming good listeners, humble facilitators, and a spark continuously igniting hope and courage in people's hearts to find their own path toward liberating love.
This journey was still long, but every small step, every enlightened soul, was an invaluable victory.
6: The echo from the “Voice of Liberated Love” platform and the initial Dialogues held by Nisa Farha and Reza Satria began creating ripples of awareness in various parts of the world. Aisha's story in Pakistan beginning to dare question her betrothal, Kenji in Japan slowly reopening the door of communication with his wife after more than two decades trapped in emotional silence, David in the United States finding relief and validation for his choice not to rush into romance, to Amara in Africa who despite facing an unsympathetic legal system no longer felt alone in her fight against domestic violence — all that was strong validation of their vision's universality. Every testimony, every small step toward self-awareness and liberation from coercion, became invaluable fuel, strengthening Nisa's and Reza's resolve that the path they chose, though steep and full of challenge, was the right path.

However, as the Cinta Merdeka Global Foundation's (YCMG) reach expanded and their interaction with diverse cultural and social realities deepened, Nisa and Reza were fully aware that the wave of transformative change they dreamed of couldn't be driven only by the two of them or by YCMG's core team based in Jakarta. A vision as big as “liberating body, soul, and knowledge” for all the world's people needed a far wider network, a global ecosystem consisting of individuals, communities, and organizations with similar concern, spirit, and commitment at the grassroots level. They needed more than just listeners or beneficiaries; they needed fellow-struggle partners, agents of change able to translate and contextualize the “Liberated Love” vision into the specific reality in their respective regions.

“We've lit small sparks in many places, Mas,” Nisa said one morning, while looking at the digital world map on the screen in their office at YCMG headquarters. That map was now filled with colorful dots marking locations where “Voice of Liberated Love” stories came from, or places where YCMG's initial programs began touching lives. “The resonance is extraordinary. Requests for dialogue, for educational modules, for counseling support, keep flowing from various corners. But to make this fire keep burning and spreading sustainably, we need more hands blowing it, more local firewood keeping it lit amid whatever cultural or political storm might come.”

Reza, reviewing the foundation's financial report and cooperation proposals from several international philanthropy foundations beginning to be interested in YCMG's approach, nodded in agreement. “You're right, Sa. Scalability and sustainability are key. We can't possibly be physically present in every village, in every community needing the 'Love Doctor's' touch. We need to build local capacity, empower leaders and agents of change at the grassroots level who truly understand the pulse of culture, language, and specific challenges in their respective regions. They'll be the real spearhead later.”

Thus, the fourth pillar was born, becoming the backbone of YCMG's long-term implementation strategy, a pillar perhaps not explicitly stated in the three initial “Liberated” pillars (Body, Soul, Knowledge), but becoming an absolute prerequisite for this movement's success and sustainability: Building a Global Network of Hope. Its focus was on carefully identifying, intensively training, sustainably supporting, and no less important, connecting in a solid ecosystem, individuals, activists, professionals (psychologists, counselors, social workers, educators, legal practitioners), community figures, and local organizations in various countries willing and having capacity to become “Love Liberation Ambassadors” or YCMG's strategic partners in their region.

The first step in building this network was launching the International “Liberated Love” Facilitator Training and Certification Program. This program was designed not just as mere technical skill training, but as a deep journey of self-transformation for its participants. This training was held online for several months, combining interactive theoretical modules on the three “Liberated” pillars (continuously updated based on research and field feedback), with group facilitation skill practice sessions, supportive and non-directive basic counseling technique, effective social change advocacy method, and sustainable community program management principles. Selected participants from various countries would get full scholarships from YCMG, with moral commitment to implement and adapt “Liberated Love” programs in their respective communities after graduating and getting certified.

The selection process for this training program's participants was done very carefully and in layers by the team led by Anton Prasetya. YCMG didn't just seek individuals with good intellectual understanding of the raised issues or relevant educational background. More than that, they sought individuals who had:
Deep Empathy: Ability to feel and understand others' suffering without judgment.
Strong Personal Integrity: Honesty, consistency between word and deed, and commitment to humanitarian values.
Cross-Cultural Communication Ability: Sensitivity and flexibility in interacting with people from diverse backgrounds.

Real Track Record: Experience, however small in scale, in doing social work, community empowerment, or advocacy on issues related to human rights, gender equality, or mental health in their environment.
Learner's Spirit: Openness to keep learning, receive feedback, and adapt to new challenges.

Hundreds, even thousands, of applications came in from various countries when the first cohort's registration opened. YCMG's selection team worked hard to screen and interview candidates. There were teachers from rural Nepal who with limited internet facility struggled to join the selection process because they wanted to teach the concept of gender equality and body rights to their female students vulnerable to child marriage. There was a young psychologist from a favela in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, who wanted to open free trauma counseling services for women and children victims of drug gang violence and domestic violence. There was an independent investigative journalist from a West African country who wanted to use his skills to expose gender-based discriminatory practices hidden within the customary legal system in his region.

One first-cohort participant whose story greatly inspired Nisa was Dr. Lena Petrova, an obstetrician and reproductive health activist from a small town in Eastern Ukraine continuously battered by armed conflict and humanitarian crisis. Lena, a tough woman in her late thirties with a gaze radiating a mix of deep sadness and steel resolve, had directly witnessed how war and displacement drastically worsened women's and children's condition. She saw how sexual violence rates skyrocketed, how many teenage girls were forced into early marriage by their families for “protection” or simply to reduce economic burden, and how access to basic reproductive health services like contraception or post-miscarriage care nearly vanished entirely. She joined YCMG's facilitator training program with one big hope: to get knowledge, skill, and international support network to build an integrated crisis service center for women and teenage girls in her region, a place they'd not only get medical care, but also psychosocial support, legal accompaniment, and empowerment to reclaim control over their life and body.

Another equally impressive participant was Rajesh Kumar, an energetic and idea-full young social worker from a densely populated slum in Mumbai, India. Rajesh, who grew up in that same environment, had dedicated his life for years to working with street children and teenagers very vulnerable to sexual exploitation, human trafficking, and drug addiction. He saw with his own eyes how lack of education about self-love, personal boundaries, healthy relationships, and sexual predator danger became the root of so many problems his students faced. He hoped YCMG's facilitator training program could give him more structured tools and methodology to give them better psychological and emotional “vaccines,” equipping them with knowledge and courage to say “no” to exploitation and build a brighter future.

There was also Fatima Al-Hassan, a young gender studies lecturer at a state university in Saudi Arabia who had quietly and at great risk long advocated women's rights through her academic writing, anonymous blog, and limited discussions with her female students. She saw YCMG's facilitator training program as a rare chance to expand her advocacy's reach, get global perspective, and most importantly, connect with an international women's activist network that could give her moral and intellectual support. Though she knew implementing the “Liberated Love” program openly in her very conservative country would be an extraordinarily heavy challenge, perhaps even endangering her safety, her spirit for change never dimmed.

That online training itself was designed by Anton Prasetya's team very interactively and participatorily. Nisa and Reza often personally gave special sessions, shared their personal experience facing political pressure or building a healthy relationship, and answered difficult questions from prospective facilitators with full honesty and humility. They didn't position themselves as all-knowing “teachers,” but as “fellow travelers” also continuing to learn.

One key message Nisa always emphasized in every session was the importance of cultural adaptation and contextualization in delivering the “Liberated Love” message. “Never try to force a model or solution from one culture to another blindly,” Nisa repeatedly told prospective facilitators. “Every community has its own local wisdom, noble values, and unique challenges. Your task isn't to replace their culture with our culture or Western culture. Your task is to become good listeners, first study the socio-cultural context where you work, identify positive values already in their tradition that could align with 'Liberated Love' principles, and find creative ways to plant seeds of awareness and empowerment from within that community itself. Be a bridge, not a bulldozer.”

Besides training individual facilitators (Love Liberation Ambassadors), YCMG also began forging strategic partnerships with local and international civil society organizations (CSOs) already having track record, credibility, and established infrastructure in the field. This partnership's main principle was mutually beneficial collaboration, not competition or co-optation. YCMG offered the “Liberated Love” concept and philosophy, tested training and education modules, access to global network and expert resources, and potential limited funding support. Meanwhile, partner CSOs provided deep local context understanding, direct access to target communities hard for YCMG to reach from Jakarta, networks with local stakeholders, and most importantly, program sustainability at the grassroots level after YCMG might no longer be intensively involved.

One early partnership that was very successful and gave significant impact was with a network of shelters (safe houses) for domestic violence victim women spread across several Latin American countries, a region with femicide and gender-based violence rates still very high. YCMG worked with managers and counselors at those shelters to integrate the “Liberated Soul” module — focused on complex trauma healing, rebuilding self-worth and confidence, developing independent life skills, and planning a violence-free future — into their holistic accompaniment program. The result was very positive. Women survivors not only got temporary physical protection, but also deeper psychological support, legal empowerment to demand justice, and skill provisions to rebuild their life stronger and with more dignity after leaving the shelter.

In several African countries, YCMG forged partnership with an international organization focused on the issue of eliminating female genital mutilation (FGM/C), a dangerous tradition still deeply rooted in many communities. YCMG not only gave financial and technical support for advocacy campaigns to change laws and social norms perpetuating FGM/C, but also developed a special “Liberated Body” program for women and girl survivors of FGM/C. This program covered education about post-trauma sexual and reproductive health, psychosexual counseling to help them cope with FGM/C's physical and psychological impact, and empowerment to reclaim rights over their body and refuse the practice for their daughters' generation. This program also involved progressive traditional figures and local religious leaders (successfully identified through the “Interfaith Dialogue” program) to together voice rejection of FGM/C from a more humanist cultural and religious perspective.

In Southeast Asia, YCMG collaborated with a regional network of teacher and educator organizations to develop and pilot teaching material about “Emotional and Relational Intelligence in Digital Context” that could be integrated into high school curriculum or extracurricular activity. This material was designed to be fun, interactive, and relevant to today's teens' life, teaching them about the importance of recognizing and managing emotion healthily, building friendship and romantic relationships based on mutual respect and consent, understanding personal boundaries and respecting others' boundaries, and how to face peer pressure, cyberbullying, and social media's negative impact on self-image and mental health. Nisa was very enthusiastic about this program, because she believed investment in character education and emotional intelligence of the young generation was key to creating a future society more just, more empathetic, and more capable of building liberating relationships.

However, building this Global Network of Hope also wasn't free from various challenges and sharp pebbles. In several countries with repressive governments or very limited civil society movement space, it was very hard for YCMG to find independent and brave local CSOs to partner with. There were also cases of unhealthy competition among local CSOs to get support or funding from YCMG, needing wisdom and firmness from Angel Marina's team in managing it. Besides, ensuring quality and integrity of facilitators or partner CSOs in the field, spread across various corners of the world with remote oversight, became homework that never finished.

Reza, with his business instinct, proposed forming a periodic accreditation and evaluation system for all Love Liberation Ambassadors and partner CSOs. “We need a minimum quality standard, Sa,” he said. “And we need a mechanism to monitor their performance, give feedback, and if needed, revoke accreditation if any are proven to misuse YCMG's name or violate our movement's basic principles.” Nisa agreed. They didn't want a movement built with noble intent tarnished by the actions of a few irresponsible bad actors. That accreditation process involved not only assessment of competence and material understanding, but also commitment to the Guard the Values Charter that had become YCMG's ethical compass.

As time passed, that Global Network of Hope began showing its strength. Love Liberation Ambassadors and partner CSOs not only became YCMG's extended hand at the local level, but also became a source of new innovation and learning for YCMG itself. They adapted YCMG's modules with local wisdom, developed new, more effective facilitation methods, and gave valuable feedback about challenges and opportunities in the field.

Dr. Lena Petrova in Eastern Ukraine, for example, succeeded in adapting YCMG's “Liberated Soul” module into an “Art Therapy for War Trauma Survivors” program, using painting, music, and dance as media for women and children to express and process their inner wounds from conflict. This program received extraordinary reception and began being replicated at several other refugee centers.

Rajesh Kumar in Mumbai, India, used the small Spark Fund he received from YCMG after graduating the facilitator training, to build a “Liberated Love Community Cafe” in the middle of the slum area where he worked. That cafe not only provided cheap and healthy food for street children, but also became a safe space for them to learn about their rights, get peer counseling, and develop their artistic talent. Rajesh also creatively used street theater performance and hip-hop music to spread “Liberated Love” messages in language easily understood by his audience.

Fatima Al-Hassan in Saudi Arabia, though facing very great risk, succeeded in forming a secret online discussion group for educated women in her country, where they could share experience, strengthen each other, and discuss women's rights concepts in a progressive Islamic perspective, inspired by YCMG's “Liberated Knowledge” material. YCMG's Guard the Values Charter, formulated together by Nisa, Reza, and the movement's pioneers in the early days, is not just a formal document hanging on the wall, but truly becomes a lived, reflected-upon, and periodically evaluated ethical guide in every interaction and decision-making. The recruitment, promotion, and performance evaluation process throughout YCMG's network always gives very heavy weight to individual behavior's alignment with these noble values.

“We can have the most brilliant program strategy and abundant financial resources,” Reza often emphasized in global orientation sessions for new staff and Ambassadors, “but if the people running it don't have sincere hearts, a straight moral compass, and sturdy personal integrity, then a movement this big and important will become fragile and easily shaken from within. The biggest legacy we can leave isn't the number of programs we run or the grandeur of the office buildings we build, but a global human community consisting of individuals of character, who truly live and fight for liberating love's values in every aspect of their lives, both personal and professional.”
Sustainable and Collaborative Systemic Change Advocacy:

YCMG realized from the start that micro-level individual empowerment alone wouldn't be enough if the bigger legal, political, economic, and socio-cultural system still perpetuated various forms of injustice, discrimination, and coercion in relationships. Therefore, YCMG's Global Advocacy and Systemic Change Division, which now has a network of human rights lawyers, public policy experts, professional lobbyists, and investigative journalists in various key countries, keeps working tirelessly to push reform of laws discriminatory toward women and minority groups, promote public policy supporting gender equality, sexual and reproductive health, and child protection, and actively fight harmful cultural narratives through smart media campaigns, constructive dialogue with opinion leaders, and support for progressive social movements at the local level.

One of YCMG's long-term advocacy focuses that will keep being a priority is ensuring that comprehensive sexuality education (CSE) and healthy and equal relationships education become an integral and mandatory part of the formal education curriculum in as many countries in the world as possible, from elementary school level to university. They believe that investment in character education, emotional intelligence, and relational literacy for the younger generation is the most fundamental key to breaking the cycle of intergenerational violence, dismantling harmful gender stereotypes, and building a healthier, more just, and more humane love culture in the future. Amid YCMG's never-truly-quiet busyness, Nisa rediscovered an old habit she'd long left behind: writing fiction. No longer with the restlessness of a single woman angry at the world like back when writing Algorithm City, this time her writing was born from a far calmer inner space. When the Sky Is No Longer the Limit, a love story behind the glitter of the entertainment world she wrote almost as a light escape between strategic meetings, actually became a kind of therapy for her — a reminder that sincere love can grow even amid the brightest public spotlight and pressure, something she'd experienced herself years ago. And Etched before It Happened, born from her deepening reflection on fate and the interconnection of six lives that initially seemed strange to each other — inspired by Surah Al-Hadid verse 22 she often contemplated before dawn — became her way of answering the question most often asked of her by Liberated Love Ambassadors: why does suffering happen, and where is God actually in the midst of it all. She never intended either to become an official YCMG statement. For Nisa, the two stories were enough to be what they were — about love and fate, written by someone who spent half her life fighting for the freedom to love, and the other half learning to accept that not everything must be fought for; some of it is enough to be trusted.

And that is Nisa Farha's and Reza Satria's greatest hope for humanity's future. A future that is warmer, brighter, more just, and more filled with liberating love. An eternal symphony that keeps resounding, inviting everyone to dance in the rhythm of universal compassion.
